questions.stem: What is the probable reason the bear walks upright on its back legs?
options: A) It tries to entertain its audience.
B) It tries to look into the distance.
C) It wants to catch people's attention.
D) It has got one of its limbs injured.

explain.定位:
Pedals apparently has an injured leg or paw that doesn't allow it to walk comfortably on all
fours according to experts.
据专家说，Pedals 似乎有一条腿或一只爪子受了伤，使它无法舒服地四肢着地行走。
explain.信号:
apparently + according to experts 引出缘由。这句靠 apparently（似乎、看来）和
according to experts（据专家说）两处信号把"原因"亮出来：新闻交代某现象的可能原因
时，常用"似乎、据专家"这种推测口吻，听到它就该锁定其所在句。
explain.替换:
has an injured leg or paw ↔ has got one of its limbs injured
leg or paw 概括为 limb
explain.排除:
A) 未提及
It tries to entertain its audience. 听起来合理（它确实成了网红），但原文从没说它"直立
是为了娱乐观众"，只说因受伤才直立，娱乐是观众的反应、不是它的动机，属凭印象的过
度联想。
B)
It tries to look into the distance. 把直立解释成"想看远处"，原文通篇没有任何"看远"的表
述，是凭"动物站起来大概为了望远"的常识硬编的原因。
C)
It wants to catch people's attention. 与原文"它确实吸引了关注、成了网红"语义沾边，所
以诱人；但题问的是"直立行走的原因"，吸引注意是结果不是原因，盗用了原文"走红、被关
注"的语义来答非所问。
借用原文：has become a social media darling

questions.stem: How is the bear first known to the public?
options: A) It was spotted by animal protection officials.
B) It was filmed by a local television reporter.
C) Its videos were posted on social media.
D) Its picture won a photography prize.

explain.定位:
The bear first gained fame after it was spotted wandering around neighborhoods and was
caught on videos that were posted on social media and shown on national television.
这只熊最初出名，是在它被发现于各个街区游荡、并被拍成视频、视频发到社交媒体上又在
全国电视上播出之后。
explain.信号:
first gained fame 直接对应题干 first known。答案句以 first gained fame（最初出名）
开头，与题干 first known to the public 严丝合缝对应，这个"first"就是定位信号：题干
问"最先"，原文哪句带 first，哪句就是答案句。
explain.替换:
caught on videos that were posted on social media ↔ Its videos were posted on social media
近乎同句的途径对应
first gained fame ↔ Its videos were posted on social media.
first gained fame 锁定该途径为"最先"
explain.排除:
A) 原词陷阱
It was spotted by animal protection officials. 借了原文反复出现的 officials 一词来骗听
感，但原文里"被发现"的是 spotted wandering around neighborhoods（在街区被发
现），officials 只是后文谈"是否转移它"的环保官员，并非"最先发现它的人"，把后文官员
安到"最初出名"上，属张冠李戴。
借用原文：Lawrence Hajna, spokesman for the state Department of Environmental Protection
B) 偷换概念
It was filmed by a local television reporter. 盗用原文 shown on national television
（在全国电视上播出）的"television"来诱选，但原文是 national（全国）电视、且只说"播
出"不是"被本地记者拍摄"；选项把"national"偷换成"local"、把"播出"偷换成"记者拍摄"，
且电视只是社媒之后的途径、非"最先"，双重不符。
借用原文：shown on national television
D) 未提及
Its picture won a photography prize. 说它"照片得了摄影奖"，原文通篇只字未提任何奖
项，是凭"网红动物大概拿过奖"的想象编出来的，原文无对应。
Questions 3 and 4 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1 It's not your imagination. Traffic in the US is actually getting worse. Americans drove more miles last
year than any other year on record. The US Department of Transportation says Americans drove nearly
3,150 billion miles last year. That's about the same distance as 337 round trips from Earth to Pluto. The
previous record was 3,003 billion miles in 2007, before the economic recession and high gas prices. The
traffic increase comes at the same time as gas prices drop significantly. The current average gas price in
the US is $1.71 per gallon. A year ago it was $2.31 per gallon and was often much higher in recent
years. A transportation expert told the reporter that job growth likely plays a part as well, along with
some people driving longer distances to and from work, and so all this means more traffic jams on the
road. The Texas A&M Travel Institute found that rush-hour travelers spent an extra 42 hours on the road
last year because of travel delays. Now, that is depressing.

options: B) The incidence of road accidents.
D) The number of people travelling.

Americans drove more miles last year than any other year on record. The US Department of
Transportation says Americans drove nearly 3,150 billion miles last year.
去年美国人开车行驶的里程比有记录以来的任何一年都多。美国交通部称，去年美国人开车
行驶了将近 31500 亿英里。
explain.信号:
纪录信号 more...than any other year on record。答案信号是『创纪录』的措辞
Americans drove more miles last year than any other year on record——more miles
than any other year（比任何一年都多）就是『打破纪录』，紧跟它的量是 miles（里
程），这句即答案句。
explain.替换:
drove more miles last year than any other year on record ↔ The distance travelled.
miles 概括为 distance travelled
explain.排除:
B) 未提及
The incidence of road accidents.（交通事故率）录音里压根没出现——通篇讲的是里
程、油价、堵车，没有一句涉及『事故』，属凭话题想当然的未提及项。
C) 原词陷阱
The spending on gas. 勾住录音里真念到的 gas 一词，制造『听到 gas 就想选』的诱惑；
但原文说 gas prices drop significantly（油价大幅下降），油价是在跌、且创纪录的是里

questions.stem: What is depressing according to the speaker?
options: C) Job growth is slowing down.

explain.定位:
The Texas A&M Travel Institute found that rush-hour travelers spent an extra 42 hours on the
road last year because of travel delays. Now, that is depressing.
得克萨斯农工大学交通研究所发现，由于交通延误，高峰期的出行者去年在路上多花了 42
个小时。这真叫人沮丧。
explain.信号:
情绪落点 that is depressing 回指上一句。答案信号是结尾的情绪词 that is depressing
——that 回指紧挨着的上一句 rush-hour travelers spent an extra 42 hours on the road
last year because of travel delays（高峰出行者多耗 42 小时），所以令人沮丧的就是
『高峰期路上耗时变多、堵车加剧』。
explain.替换:
rush-hour travelers spent an extra 42 hours on the road ↔ Rush-hour traffic is worsening.
多耗时=交通在恶化，详述换概括
because of travel delays ↔ Rush-hour traffic is worsening.
travel delays 印证 traffic worsening
explain.排除:
A) 与原文相反
Fewer people are commuting. 说『通勤的人变少』，但原文讲的是 some people
driving longer distances to and from work（有人上下班开得更远）、整体里程创纪录，
路上是更挤而非更空，方向正好相反。
借用原文：some people driving longer distances to and from work
B) 原词陷阱
Gas consumption is soaring. 勾住录音念到的 gas；但原文只说 gas prices drop
significantly（油价大降），讲的是『油价下跌』，从没说『油耗飙升』，且 depressing
也不是冲着油来的，答非所问。
借用原文：gas prices drop significantly
C) 原词陷阱
Job growth is slowing down. 偷了录音原句里的 job growth；但原文是 job growth
likely plays a part，说就业增长是导致开车变多的一个原因（即就业在增长），并非『放
缓』，也不是 depressing 所指，方向与考点都不对。
借用原文：job growth likely plays a part

carrying man\'s groceries to his car ↔ carry groceries to his car

questions.stem: When the author was a college student, she found that knitting helped her concentrate.
questions.passage:
The Health Benefits of Knitting

A) About 15 years ago, I was invited to join a knitting group. I agreed to give it a try.

B) My mother had taught me to knit at 15, and I knitted in class throughout college and for a few years thereafter. Then decades passed without my touching a knitting needle. But within two Mondays in the group, I was hooked, not only on knitting but also on crocheting(钩织), and I was on my way to becoming a highly productive crafter.

C) I've made countless baby blankets, sweaters, scarves, hats and caps for newborns. I take a knitting project with me everywhere, especially when I have to sit still and listen. As I discovered in college, when my hands are busy, my mind stays focused on the here and now.

D) It seems, too, that I'm part of a national renewal of interest in needle and other handicrafts(手工艺). The Craft Yarn Council reports that a third of women ages 25-35 now knit or crochet. Even men and schoolchildren are swelling the ranks, among them my friend's three small grandsons. Last April, the council created a "Stitch Away Stress" campaign in honor of National Stress Awareness Month. Dr. Herbert Benson, a pioneer in mind/body medicine and author of The Relaxation Response, says that the repetitive action of needlework can induce a relaxed state like that associated with meditation(沉思) and yoga. questions.passage:
For the past several decades, it seems there's been a general consensus on how to get ahead in America: Get a college education, find a reliable job, and buy your own home. But do Americans still believe in that path, and if they do, is it attainable?

The most recent National Journal poll asked respondents about the American dream, what it takes to achieve their goals, and whether or not they felt a significant amount of control over their ability to be successful. Overwhelmingly, the results show that today, the idea of the American dream—and what it takes to achieve it—looks quite different than it did in the late 20th century.

By and large, people felt that their actions and hard work—not outside forces—were the deciding factor in how their lives turned out. But respondents had decidedly mixed feelings about what actions make for a better life in current economy.

In the last seven years, Americans have grown more pessimistic about the power of education to lead to success. Even though they see going to college as a fairly achievable goal, a majority—52 percent—think that young people do not need a four-year college education in order to be successful.

Miguel Maeda, 42, who has a master's degree and works in public health, was the first in his family to go to college, which has allowed him to achieve a sense of financial stability his parents and grandparents never did.

While some, like Maeda, emphasized the value of the degree rather than the education itself, others still see college as a way to gain new perspectives and life experiences.

Sixty-year-old Will Fendley, who had a successful career in the military and never earned a college degree, thinks "personal drive" is far more important than just going to college. To Fendley, a sense of drive and purpose, as well as an effective high-school education, and basic life skills, like balancing a checkbook, are the necessary ingredients for a successful life in America.

questions.stem: What do Americans now think of the role of college education in achieving success?
options: A) It still remains open to debate.
B) It has proved to be beyond doubt.
C) It is no longer as important as it used to be.
D) It is much better understood now than ever.
questions.passage:
For the past several decades, it seems there's been a general consensus on how to get ahead in America: Get a college education, find a reliable job, and buy your own home. But do Americans still believe in that path, and if they do, is it attainable?

The most recent National Journal poll asked respondents about the American dream, what it takes to achieve their goals, and whether or not they felt a significant amount of control over their ability to be successful. Overwhelmingly, the results show that today, the idea of the American dream—and what it takes to achieve it—looks quite different than it did in the late 20th century.

By and large, people felt that their actions and hard work—not outside forces—were the deciding factor in how their lives turned out. But respondents had decidedly mixed feelings about what actions make for a better life in current economy.

In the last seven years, Americans have grown more pessimistic about the power of education to lead to success. Even though they see going to college as a fairly achievable goal, a majority—52 percent—think that young people do not need a four-year college education in order to be successful.

Miguel Maeda, 42, who has a master's degree and works in public health, was the first in his family to go to college, which has allowed him to achieve a sense of financial stability his parents and grandparents never did.

While some, like Maeda, emphasized the value of the degree rather than the education itself, others still see college as a way to gain new perspectives and life experiences.

Sixty-year-old Will Fendley, who had a successful career in the military and never earned a college degree, thinks "personal drive" is far more important than just going to college. To Fendley, a sense of drive and purpose, as well as an effective high-school education, and basic life skills, like balancing a checkbook, are the necessary ingredients for a successful life in America.

中所起的作用」。无陷阱。

writing.model:
The relationship between teachers and students lies at the heart of effective learning. Rather than merely
arguing that it matters, I believe the real question is how to best handle it. In my view, mutual respect, equal
communication and teaching each other are the keys.
First and foremost, both sides should treat each other as equals. A teacher who patiently listens to opinions, and
a student who genuinely values guidance, can build trust rather than distance. In addition, honest and timely
communication clears up misunderstandings; for instance, students who raise their questions after class often
find the lessons far easier to follow.

dialogue. Once teachers and students handle their relationship in this way, both teaching and learning will
become truly rewarding.
